evidence.claim: Interlake Road leaves Jolon Road just south of Lockwood and runs toward Lake San Antonio.
evidence.quote: As Interlake Road, G14 heads west with a brief curve to the north for a few miles, passing Bee Rock and Lake San Antonio before turning mainly northwest and eventually north towards the town of Lockwood.

evidence.claim: At the Lockwood end, farms, cattle ranches and vineyards occupy a broad valley enclosed by coastal mountains.
evidence.quote: It is a small community consisting of farms, ranches, and vineyards, in a broad valley encompassed by the coastal mountains.

evidence.claim: Caltrans recognizes the section from Jolon Road to the San Luis Obispo County line as an officially designated County Scenic Highway.
evidence.quote: INTERLAKE RD from JOLON RD in Lockwood to the SLO COUNTY 1971 5 LUIS OBISPO LINE

evidence.claim: That designation dates to 1971; the adjoining Interlake Road–Nacimiento Drive segment received its own designation in 1972.
evidence.quote: INTERLAKE RD from JOLON RD in Lockwood to the SLO COUNTY 1971 5 LUIS OBISPO LINE MONTEREY/SAN INTERLAKE RD-NACIMIENTO DRIVE from the MONTEREY 1972

evidence.claim: The lake had already changed the valley: San Antonio Dam was completed in 1965, and the reservoir submerged the town of Pleyto.
evidence.quote: The dam is 202 feet (62 m) tall and was completed in 1965

evidence.claim: The reservoir’s main purpose is groundwater supply, keeping water in the river through the year so it can seep into the ground.
evidence.quote: Lake San Antonio's primary purpose is to provide groundwater. Without the lake, the San Antonio River would be nearly dry in the summer months. With water in the river year-round, more of it can seep into the ground.

evidence.claim: Begin at the Jolon Road junction south of Lockwood, where Interlake Road carries the G14 county-route number.
evidence.quote: Just a few hundred feet (~100 meters) south of Lockwood, G14 reaches the intersection of the western terminus of CR G18 and heads west along Jolon Road.

evidence.claim: Follow it south toward Lake San Antonio and the county line.
evidence.quote: passing Bee Rock and Lake San Antonio before turning mainly northwest and eventually north towards the town of Lockwood.

evidence.claim: Beyond this segment, the separately designated scenic road continues to Chimney Rock Road in San Luis Obispo County.
evidence.quote: INTERLAKE RD-NACIMIENTO DRIVE from the MONTEREY 1972 5 LUIS OBISPO COUNTY LINE to CHIMNEY ROCK RD in San Luis Obispo County

evidence.claim: Lockwood’s name honors Belva Lockwood, the Equal Rights Party’s presidential candidate in 1884 and 1888.
evidence.quote: The name honors Belva Lockwood, candidate for President of the United States in 1884 and 1888 on the Equal Rights Party ticket.

evidence.claim: The community’s first post office opened in 1888, the year of her second campaign.
evidence.quote: The first post office opened in 1888.

evidence.claim: The setting is a broad valley surrounded by coastal mountains, with farms, ranches and vineyards.
evidence.quote: It is a small community consisting of farms, ranches, and vineyards, in a broad valley encompassed by the coastal mountains.

evidence.claim: San Antonio Valley Vineyards are part of the community, along with olive groves and extensive land for cattle grazing.
evidence.quote: Lockwood also encompasses the San Antonio Valley Vineyards, including several more vineyards and a few olive groves. There is extensive grazing land and cattle ranching in the area

evidence.claim: A post office and community center serve Lockwood.
evidence.quote: There is a post office in Lockwood and a community center.

evidence.claim: The town lies nine miles northwest of Lake San Antonio and six miles east-southeast of Jolon, in southern Monterey County.
evidence.quote: It is 9 miles (14 km) northwest of Lake San Antonio

evidence.claim: Much of Rancho Pleyto is beneath Lake San Antonio, including the later town of Pleyto.
evidence.quote: Much of the grant is under water, inundated by the creation of the San Antonio Reservoir.

evidence.claim: Governor Pío Pico granted the land to Antonio Chaves in 1845; it extended along the San Antonio River southeast of Jolon.
evidence.quote: It was granted in 1845 by Governor Pío Pico to Antonio Chaves (Chávez).   The grant extended along the San Antonio River southeast of present-day Jolon.

evidence.claim: After California passed to the United States, a claim for the grant was filed with the Public Land Commission in 1852.
evidence.quote: a claim for Rancho Pleyto was filed with the Public Land Commission in 1852

evidence.claim: William Pinkerton bought a large portion in 1868 and founded Pleyto.
evidence.quote: William Pinkerton (1843–1918) bought a large portion of Rancho Pleyto in 1868, and founded the town of Pleyto

evidence.claim: The grant was patented to William S. Johnson and Preston K. Woodside in 1872.
evidence.quote: the grant was patented to William S. Johnson and Preston K. Woodside in 1872.

evidence.quote: Lake San Antonio's primary purpose is to provide groundwater.

evidence.quote: Without the lake, the San Antonio River would be nearly dry in the summer months.

flags: Caltrans verifies the 1971 county scenic designation and endpoints, but gives no designation rationale or road-building history. Cache describes the agricultural valley and route direction, not drive time, overlooks, or detailed grades. Overview is shorter than requested to avoid padding.
Both current moments and their location metadata retained. No factual current claim was dropped for lack of support; supported Belva Lockwood and groundwater details remain.

Added Rancho Pleyto as historical context for the lake. Its coordinates are copied from the cached Wikipedia page and indicate a historical area, not a verified visitor stop or visible ruins. Ordered between Lockwood and the reservoir using cached geography; material has no lake or rancho mile. The separate-excursion category must not imply present site access.

The Lake San Antonio cache reports a 2024 recreational closure after a fish die-off but gives no reopening date or current access confirmation. No present boating, camping, or park-entry promise is made. Editor should verify access before publishing visitor logistics.
The county-routes source broadly calls G14 a State Scenic Highway. Used Caltrans’s more precise County Scenic Highway designation for these two limited segments, not for the whole numbered route.
Rancho Los Ojitos source says the grant is mostly beneath the lake but also describes military ownership; omitted this unresolved geography rather than treating it as a second submerged site.
